subsystems.name: Target-tissue access
subsystems.role: getting an editor to the right cells — melanocytes in the skin, or bone-forming cells and growth-plate cartilage in the skeleton.
parts: blood supply to the target tissue

subsystems.name: Editing payload
subsystems.role: the molecular tool that rewrites a chosen gene.

subsystems.name: Delivery vehicle
subsystems.role: carries the payload into cells without triggering immunity.

subsystems.name: Control and dosing
subsystems.role: decides how much editing happens, where, and whether it can be stopped.

subsystems.name: Verification and safety
subsystems.role: confirms the intended edit and screens for unintended ones.

buildSteps.title: Pick the trait genes
buildSteps.detail: Choose genes with well-understood, dose-sensitive effects — for pigment, the melanin pathway genes such as MC1R, SLC24A5 and OCA2; for bone, genes in growth-plate and osteoblast signalling.

buildSteps.title: Design the editor
buildSteps.detail: Write a guide RNA against the chosen site and choose an editor: a base editor changes one letter without cutting DNA, which is safer than a nuclease that makes a double-strand break.

buildSteps.title: Build the delivery vehicle
buildSteps.detail: Encapsulate the payload in lipid nanoparticles or engineer a viral capsid that preferentially infects skin or bone cells rather than the liver.

buildSteps.title: Deliver to the target
buildSteps.detail: Inject locally into skin, or infuse systemically; repeat doses may be needed because only a fraction of cells take up the payload.

buildSteps.title: Edit the cells
buildSteps.detail: Inside the target cell the editor binds its DNA site and rewrites it. Pigment changes would show within weeks as skin renews; bone changes would take far longer.

buildSteps.title: Verify and monitor
buildSteps.detail: Biopsy the tissue and sequence it to measure how many cells were edited and to check for off-target changes, then track the visible trait over months.

buildSteps.title: Manage safety
buildSteps.detail: Watch for immune reactions to the vehicle, and for cancer risk if dividing cells were edited; plan for reversibility, which permanent edits do not offer.

buildSteps.title: Scale to a controlled procedure
buildSteps.detail: Turn the one-off experiment into a reproducible protocol with defined dose, follow-up and the ability to correct mistakes.

prerequisites.tech: Somatic gene editing inside the body
prerequisites.why: liver-targeting lipid nanoparticles have edited genes in patients in trials, but reaching skin and bone is much harder.
the melanin pathway is well mapped, so a pigment change is at least a defined target.

prerequisites.tech: Control of adult bone growth and shape
prerequisites.why: adult bone is remodelled slowly; there is no established way to reshape a skeleton by editing genes.
current vehicles concentrate in the liver; directing them to melanocytes or osteoblasts is unsolved.

prerequisites.tech: Long-term safety data for permanent edits
prerequisites.why: edits that persist for life carry cancer and immune risks that decades of follow-up must rule out.

pathway.milestone: approved ex vivo editing therapies for blood disorders (from 2023) and gene-corrected skin grafts for blistering skin disease
pathway.unlocks: proof that editing human cells can treat disease safely enough to approve.

pathway.milestone: in-body editing of organs beyond the liver, including skin
pathway.unlocks: the first realistic route to changing a visible trait.

pathway.milestone: editing for non-medical traits, starting with pigment
pathway.unlocks: the regulatory and ethical fight over enhancement, not just treatment.
only if bone remodelling can be driven safely over months — otherwise this stays speculation, since adult bone structure is not a software setting.
